passages.happening:
One Sabbath Jesus is walking through the grainfields. His disciples pick heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat them.

Some of the Pharisees ask, “Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” (verse 2).

Jesus reminds them of David. When David and his men were hungry, he went into the house of God, took the consecrated bread, which only priests were allowed to eat, and shared it with his companions. Then Jesus says, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this story too (Mark 2:23-28; Matthew 12:1-8), and their notes explain it more fully. The problem was not that the disciples took someone else's grain. The law let a hungry traveller pick grain by hand from a neighbour's field (Deuteronomy 23:25). The problem was the day. The law named harvest time in particular as work to rest from (Exodus 34:21). Later, around AD 200, Jewish teaching written down in the Mishnah listed reaping and threshing among the kinds of work not allowed on the Sabbath. Picking grain and rubbing it in the hands looked like a small harvest.

Only Luke mentions the rubbing. And Luke says ‘some of the Pharisees’ asked, not all of them.

The Pharisees were not monsters. They loved the Sabbath and wanted to protect it. That is what makes the clash serious.
passages.ot:
The story of David is in 1 Samuel 21:1-6. The priest gave him “the consecrated bread” (1 Samuel 21:6), the loaves set out before God each week, which the law kept for the priests (Leviticus 24:5-9). Need came before the rule.

The Sabbath was a gift and a sign: “a sign between Me and you” (Exodus 31:13). God gave it for rest and for joy. Isaiah called it “a delight” (Isaiah 58:13).
passages.hard: Did Jesus break the Sabbath? He never said the Sabbath did not matter, and he kept it, as Luke shows (4:16). What he challenged was a reading of the rules that left hungry people hungry. And then he made a much larger claim. ‘Lord of the Sabbath’ means he has the right to say what God's day is for. Only the one who gave the Sabbath could say that.
passages.asks: Rules can be good gifts, and they can also be used to keep people from what they need. Where do you hold to a rule in a way that leaves someone hungry? And is Jesus Lord of your day of rest, or only the rules about it?

passages.t: A hand restored on the Sabbath
passages.happening:
On another Sabbath Jesus is teaching in a synagogue. A man is there whose right hand is withered. The scribes and Pharisees watch closely to see if Jesus will heal on the Sabbath, so that they can accuse him.

Jesus knows their thoughts. He tells the man, “Get up and stand among us” (verse 8). Then he asks them, “I ask you, which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” (verse 9).

He looks around at all of them and tells the man, “Stretch out your hand” (verse 10). The man does, and his hand is made well. The scribes and Pharisees are filled with rage and begin to discuss what they might do to Jesus.
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too (Mark 3:1-6; Matthew 12:9-14). Only Luke says it was the man's right hand. For most people that was the working hand. A man who could not use it might not be able to earn a living.

Jesus makes the man stand in the middle, where everyone can see. He does not heal him quietly in a corner.

Jewish teachers agreed that saving a life came before the Sabbath. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, later than the Gospels, says that even a doubt about danger to life sets the Sabbath aside (Yoma 8:6). But this man was not dying. He could have waited a day. That is the point of Jesus' question. To leave someone in need when you could help him is not neutral. On God's day, doing good is never out of place.
passages.ot: The prophets said God wants mercy more than empty ritual: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). Micah asked what God requires, and answered, “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard: Are these scenes fair to the Pharisees? Luke says some of them were filled with rage. But the Gospels also show Pharisees who invite Jesus to eat (7:36), who warn him of danger (13:31), and who later speak for the apostles (Acts 5:34-39). Paul was one. The Pharisees were not all alike, and the debate about the Sabbath was a real debate about honouring God's command. The danger the story shows is one every religious person faces: caring more about a rule than about the person in front of you.
passages.asks: The man had to stand up in front of a room full of watching people. Jesus put him in the centre. Is there someone in your church or circle who has been on the edge, whom Jesus would bring into the middle? And when you could do good today, what keeps you waiting?

passages.t: A night of prayer, and twelve chosen
passages.happening:
Jesus goes out to the mountain to pray, and he spends the whole night in prayer to God.

When daylight comes, he calls his disciples and chooses twelve of them, “whom He also designated as apostles” (verse 13). They are Simon, whom he names Peter, and his brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus and Simon called the Zealot; Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew give this list too (Mark 3:13-19; Matthew 10:1-4), and their notes explain the names. Twelve was not a random number. Israel was made up of twelve tribes. By choosing twelve, Jesus signals that he is gathering and renewing God's people.

Only Luke says Jesus prayed all night first. It is one of the many times Luke shows Jesus praying before a turning point (3:21; 9:18; 9:29). The choice of the twelve came out of prayer.

‘Apostle’ comes from a Greek word meaning ‘one who is sent’. A disciple is a learner. An apostle is a learner sent out with a message.

The lists do not quite match. Where Matthew and Mark name Thaddaeus, Luke and Acts name ‘Judas son of James’ (Acts 1:13). Most think these are two names for one man, but the Gospels do not say so.

Simon the Zealot, a name for someone burning with zeal for God's law, sits beside Matthew, a tax collector (Matthew 10:3). A man who might once have hated Rome and a man who had worked for its rulers are in the same band.
passages.ot:
Moses also went up a mountain and came down to the people with God's word (Exodus 19). Jesus goes up a mountain to pray, chooses twelve, and then comes down to teach.

Prayer before choosing leaders is an old pattern. When the apostles had to replace Judas, they prayed first (Acts 1:24). The psalms ask God to guide: “Teach me Your way, O LORD” (Psalm 27:11).
passages.hard: Why would Jesus choose Judas, after a night of prayer? Luke does not explain, and the list does not hide it: ‘who became a traitor’. Notice Luke's words: Judas became a traitor. He was not one when he was chosen. The Gospels show Jesus giving Judas the same calling, the same teaching, and the same place at the table as the rest. The betrayal was Judas's own choice, not a lack of welcome.
passages.asks: Jesus prayed all night before a decision. What decisions are in front of you, and have you prayed about them for even an hour? Notice too the mixed group he chose: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot. Jesus' people have never been all of one kind.

passages.t: Blessings and woes on a level place
passages.happening:
Jesus comes down with the twelve and stands on a level place. A large crowd of disciples is there, and a great number of people from all over Judea, from Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon. They have come to hear him and to be healed. Everyone tries to touch him, “because power was coming from Him and healing them all” (verse 19).

Looking up at his disciples, Jesus says:

“Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (verse 20). “Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (verse 21). The same is true of those who are hated, shut out and insulted because of the Son of Man. They should leap for joy, because their reward in heaven is great. Their persecutors' ancestors treated the prophets the same way.

“But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort” (verse 24). Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. Woe to you when everyone speaks well of you, for their ancestors treated the false prophets the same way.
passages.hearers:
This is the start of Luke's great sermon, often called the Sermon on the Plain. Matthew has a longer sermon, given on a mountain, in chapters 5 to 7 (the Sermon on the Mount), and its notes explain much of what follows. Many readers think the two Gospels give the same sermon, each shaped in its own way. Others think Jesus taught these things more than once, in different places, as travelling teachers do. Both views are held by careful readers.

Notice the crowd. It includes people from Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the coast. Luke, who has just told of the widow of Zarephath in Sidon (4:26), shows the outsiders coming already.

A saying that begins ‘Blessed are’ was familiar from the Psalms. It is not a wish. It is a statement about someone's condition before God, something like ‘how well off they are’ or ‘God's favour is on them’.

Luke's list differs from Matthew's. Matthew has eight blessings, and all speak of ‘those who’. Luke has four, spoken straight to the hearers, ‘you’. And Luke adds four ‘woes’, which Matthew does not have. Each woe is the mirror of a blessing: poor and rich, hungry and full, weeping and laughing, hated and praised.

‘Woe’ is not a curse. It is a cry of grief and warning, something like ‘How sad for you’ or ‘Watch out’. The prophets used it often.

Luke's word for ‘poor’ usually meant the very poor: people with nothing, even beggars. It was the word for the opposite of rich.
passages.ot:
The prophets pronounced woes on the rich who took land from the poor: “Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field” (Isaiah 5:8). They also warned against false prophets everyone liked, who said “‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace at all” (Jeremiah 6:14). Israel's true prophets were often hated by their own people (4:24).

The promises come from the Psalms and the Prophets. “Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5). Isaiah's messenger was sent with good news to the poor and comfort for those who mourn, the very reading Jesus gave at Nazareth (4:18).

The wise man of Proverbs prayed, “Give me neither poverty nor riches” (Proverbs 30:8), because too much might make him forget God, and too little might make him steal. Scripture knows the dangers of both.
passages.hard:
‘Blessed are you who are poor’ and ‘Woe to you who are rich’. Does Luke mean money, or the heart? Both, and it matters how they fit.

Matthew has “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3). Luke has “Blessed are you who are poor” (verse 20). Luke's wording is plainer, and it should not be blunted. He means people who are really poor, who have little food and no security. God has a special care for those who have nothing. That runs through the whole of Luke's Gospel, from Mary's song to the beggar Lazarus.

But Luke does not say that being poor makes anyone good, or that poverty is holy in itself. Jesus is ‘looking up at His disciples’ when he speaks. These are poor people who have come to him. The kingdom is theirs because they belong to him, not because they are poor. Matthew's ‘in spirit’ names the heart that goes with it: people who know they have nothing to bring God. The two Gospels do not contradict each other. Luke stresses the outward state, Matthew the inward one, and both are true.

The woe on the rich is just as plain, and it is a warning, not contempt. ‘You have already received your comfort’ means that the rich can come to have nothing to look forward to but what they already hold. Wealth in Luke is more often a danger than a reward, so these words turn upside down the idea that money is a sign of God's blessing. But Luke does not despise the rich either. Women of means support Jesus from what they own (8:3). Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector, is welcomed (19:8-9). When the disciples ask who then can be saved, Jesus says, “What is impossible with man is possible with God” (18:27). Every reader, rich or poor, is asked where their comfort lies.

The blessing on those who are hated ‘because of the Son of Man’ is not a call to seek suffering, or to treat every hard word as persecution. It is a promise to those who suffer because they belong to Jesus.
passages.asks: If you are poor, hungry or grieving, hear Jesus speak to you directly: you are not forgotten, and your story does not end here. If you are comfortable, well fed and well liked, hear the warning with the same seriousness: where is your comfort? Most readers are some of both. Which words do you most need to hear today?

passages.happening:
Jesus goes on: “But to those of you who will listen, I say: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you” (verses 27-28).

If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other. If someone takes your cloak, do not hold back your tunic. Give to everyone who asks, and if someone takes what is yours, do not demand it back. “Do to others as you would have them do to you” (verse 31).

If you love only those who love you, what credit is that? Even sinners do that. If you lend only where you expect to be repaid, sinners do that too. “But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return” (verse 35). Then you will be children of the Most High, “for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked” (verse 35). “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Matthew gives much of this in his chapter 5, and its notes explain the cheek, the cloak and the tunic. A tunic was the long shirt worn next to the skin; a cloak was the outer coat, which also served as a blanket at night.

Luke tells the cloak picture differently. In Matthew someone sues you for your tunic, and you let him have your cloak too (Matthew 5:40), a scene in court. In Luke someone grabs your cloak, and you do not hold back your tunic, a scene of robbery in the street. Either way, Jesus asks his followers not to hit back.

Luke's version of the ‘golden rule’ comes in the middle, with no mention of the Law and the Prophets. A famous Jewish teacher named Hillel is said to have taught a negative form of it: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. That saying is recorded in the Talmud, written down centuries later. Jesus puts it positively: do not only avoid harm, do the good you would want.

Lending was a real issue. Poor farmers often had to borrow to get through a bad year. Jesus says to lend even to enemies, without counting on getting it back.

Where Matthew says ‘Be perfect’ (Matthew 5:48), Luke says ‘Be merciful’. Mercy is what God's perfection looks like toward people who do not deserve it.
passages.ot:
The law already said, “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). It told Israel to return an enemy's stray ox (Exodus 23:4), and Proverbs said, “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat” (Proverbs 25:21). Moses told Israel to lend freely to a poor neighbour (Deuteronomy 15:8). Jesus takes these and pushes them all the way: love the enemy as the Father does.

God's own kindness to the ungrateful is the pattern. Israel's history is a long story of God being kind to a people who often forgot him.
passages.hard:
Christians have read ‘turn the other cheek’ in three main ways. Pacifists, such as the Anabaptists and their heirs the Mennonites, read it as forbidding all violence. Martin Luther taught two kinds of duty: in your own cause, bear wrong without revenge, but a ruler or judge must protect others and punish wrong (Romans 13:4). The just war tradition, from Augustine to Thomas Aquinas, holds that love of neighbor can require lawful force to protect the innocent, within strict limits. These notes do not decide between them.

One thing must be said plainly. ‘Turn the other cheek’ is not a command to stay with someone who is hurting you. Jesus speaks of refusing revenge, not of accepting abuse. When an officer struck him, Jesus asked, “why did you strike Me?” (John 18:23). Paul used his rights under Roman law to stop a flogging (Acts 22:25). Seeking safety, and the protection of the law, is not disobedience to Jesus. If you are being harmed, tell someone you trust and get help.

Loving an enemy does not mean pretending they did no wrong, or trusting someone who is still dangerous. It means wanting their good, praying for them, and refusing to wish them harm. In the same way, ‘give to everyone who asks’ is a call to a generous, open hand. It is not a rule that you must hand over what will be used to harm you or others.
passages.asks: Jesus asks for a love that goes beyond what anyone would expect, the love God has shown to us. Think of one person who has wronged you. What would it mean to pray for them by name this week, and to wish them good, while still keeping yourself safe? And who could you help without expecting anything back?

passages.t: Do not judge; the speck and the beam
passages.happening:
“Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (verse 37). Give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, poured into your lap. “For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you” (verse 38).

Jesus tells a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?” (verse 39). A student is not above his teacher, but a fully trained student will be like his teacher.

Why look at the speck in your brother's eye and miss the beam in your own? You cannot offer to take out his speck while a beam is in your eye. “You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye” (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
Matthew has the speck and the beam too (Matthew 7:1-5), and its notes explain the picture. The speck is a chip of straw or wood. The beam is a roof timber. The picture is meant to make people laugh: a man with a plank sticking out of his eye, offering to do delicate work on someone else's.

The measure is a picture from the market. People had no pockets. A fold of the robe above the belt could hold things, and grain could be poured into it. Jesus pictures a seller who does not cheat but fills the measure, presses it down, shakes it to make room, and pours until it spills over into your lap. God is generous like that, and the way you treat others is the way you will be treated.

The blind guide and the student fit here. You can only lead others as far as you can see. A student becomes like the teacher. So a teacher who judges harshly will train students who judge harshly.
passages.ot: God alone sees the heart: “I, the LORD, search the heart” (Jeremiah 17:10). That is why condemning others is dangerous. The law also asked for honest measures in the market (Leviticus 19:35-36). Jesus turns the honest measure into a picture of God's generosity.
passages.hard:
Do not judge? Does Jesus mean Christians may never say that anything is wrong? Most readers say no, and the passage itself shows why. In verse 42 Jesus expects the brother's speck to be removed, once your own eye is clear. And in the next verses he tells his hearers to know a tree by its fruit. What Jesus forbids is the judging that condemns, that looks down, that sees others' faults and never one's own. Paul says to restore someone who has fallen “with a spirit of gentleness” and to watch yourself (Galatians 6:1).

Verse 38 is sometimes used to promise money in return for giving money, often to a ministry. That is not what it means. The setting is mercy, forgiveness and lending to enemies without expecting anything back. God's overflowing measure is his mercy, not a payout.
passages.asks: It is easier to see what is wrong with someone else than with yourself. Who are you quick to judge? Before you speak to them, ask what beam might be in your own eye. And ask whether people around you would describe you as a person who forgives, or one who keeps score.

passages.t: Trees and fruit, the heart and the mouth
passages.happening:
“No good tree bears bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit” (verse 43). Each tree is known by its fruit. People do not pick figs from thornbushes or grapes from brambles.

“The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks” (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
Figs and grapes were everyday fruit in Israel. Thornbushes and brambles grew on every hillside. Anyone could tell them apart by what they produced.

Matthew uses the tree picture to warn about false prophets (Matthew 7:15-20). Luke puts it right after the speck and the beam. In Luke it is about every disciple. You cannot judge others well until your own heart is good, because what you say shows what is inside you.

‘The heart’, in the Bible, is not only feelings. It is the centre of a person: thoughts, choices, desires and loves. A ‘treasure’ here is a storeroom. What is stored up comes out.
passages.ot: The psalm pictures the person who loves God's word as “a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season” (Psalm 1:3). God promised through Ezekiel a new heart: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). Good fruit does not come from trying harder on the outside. It comes from a heart God has made new.
passages.hard: Does this mean people are either all good or all bad? No one in Scripture is simply good, except God (18:19). The picture is about where a life comes from. Jesus is not sorting people into two fixed groups. He is saying that the root shapes the fruit, and so the change he brings starts with the heart.
passages.asks: Listen to yourself for a day. What do your words show about what is stored in your heart? If you do not like what you hear, the answer is not only to be careful with your tongue, but to ask God to change the storeroom.

passages.happening:
“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but not do what I say?” (verse 46).

Jesus describes the one who comes to him, hears his words and acts on them. He is like a man building a house who “dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock” (verse 48). When the flood came, the torrent crashed against the house but could not shake it, because it was well built.

But the one who hears and does not act is like a man who built his house on ground with no foundation. The torrent hit it, and it fell at once, and it was utterly destroyed.
passages.hearers:
Matthew ends his sermon the same way (Matthew 7:24-27), and its notes explain the picture. Israel's rains came in their seasons, and a heavy storm could send torrents through low ground. A house with no foundation would be undercut.

Luke's telling has its own detail. Matthew speaks of one house on rock and one on sand. Luke speaks of one builder who dug deep, down to the rock, and one who did not dig at all. From the outside, both houses may have looked the same. The difference was below ground, in work no one could see. Only the flood showed it.

‘Lord, Lord’ was a title of honour. Jesus says the title means nothing if his words are ignored.
passages.ot: The wise man of Proverbs said, “When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever” (Proverbs 10:25). Isaiah spoke of God laying “a stone in Zion” for a sure foundation (Isaiah 28:16). In the Psalms God himself is the rock of his people (Psalm 18:2).
passages.hard: Is Jesus saying we are saved by how well we obey? The sermon began with blessings given to the poor before they had done anything. The foundation is Jesus and his words. Obeying them is how a person builds on that foundation, not how they buy it. But Jesus is clear that hearing without doing is a house waiting to fall.
passages.asks: Everyone faces a flood sooner or later: grief, illness, failure, temptation. What are you building on? Pick one thing Jesus says in this chapter, love your enemies, do not judge, give without expecting back, and dig down by doing it this week.
